<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. Adelita S. Grijalva>: Joint employment is a flashpoint in labor and employment law because of the recent trend toward ``fissuring,'' or the disintegration of the firm through the use of overlapping arrangements of contracting, subcontracting, franchising, and temping.\21\ Fissuring is increasingly common in low wage industries, including but not limited to logistics,\22\ food service, retail, and janitorial services.\23\ Today, there are nearly 9 million Americans working at over 800,000 individual franchises.\24\ Fissured work arrangements are associated with increased incidence of a host of workplace violations.\25\
\21\See generally David Weil, The Fissured Workplace: Why Work Became So Bad for So Many and What Can Be Done to Improve It (2014).
\22\See, e.g., Stacy Mitchell & Olivia LaVecchia, Amazon's Stranglehold: How the Company's Tightening Grip Is Stifling Competition, Eroding Jobs, and Threatening Communities (Nov. 2016), https://ilsr.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/ ILSR_AmazonReport_final.pdf.
\23\See Catherine Ruckelshaus et al., Who's the Boss: Restoring Accountability for Labor Standards in Outsourced Work, Nat'l Emp. Law Proj. (May 7, 2014), https://www.nelp.org/app/uploads/2015/02/Whos-the- Boss-Restoring-Accountability-Labor-Standards-Outsourced-Work- Report.pdf.
\24\Franchising Economic Outlook, Int'l Franchise Ass'n (2026), https://indd.adobe.com/view/c09364f3-8c80-4b2f-bbcc-56414924ae67.
\25\Weil, supra note 21.
The rise of the ``fissured workplace'' makes FLSA enforcement challenging. For example, it can be difficult for workers experiencing wage theft at the bottom of a chain of contracts to collect stolen wages when the nominal employer is a fly-by-night staffing company. In such a case, the joint employer theory allows workers to seek their stolen wages from a larger company further up that chain, if that larger company shares power over the terms of employment.
Fissuring can also weaken workers' bargaining power. Absent the joint employment doctrine, workers hired by an intermediary firm but laboring for a larger, more powerful firm with actual control over their working conditions and wages will find it difficult to bargain meaningfully.
THE FRANCHISE MODEL AND JOINT EMPLOYMENT
In the franchise business model, the corporate parent or ``franchisor'' allows an independent business owner, or franchisee, to use its branding, business model, and other intellectual property. In return, the franchisee agrees to pay an upfront franchise fee, ongoing royalties, and is subject to the terms of the franchise agreement that sets operating, performance, and management standards for the franchisee.\26\
\26\Introduction to the Franchise Business Model, Int'l Franchise Ass'n, https://www.franchise.org/franchising-overview/introduction-to-the-franchise-business-model/ (last visited Aug. 19, 2026).
Despite claims that franchisees operate as independent small businesses, corporate franchisors can and do exercise significant amount of control over their franchisees. Through franchise agreements, brand standards, and operational requirements, franchisors often set operating hours, mandate staffing levels, require specific scheduling or payroll software, establish detailed rules for how work must be performed, and restrict who may work under a franchise agreement. For example, some fast-food franchisors provide their franchises with extensive operation manuals that set franchise requirements on everything from workers' training, dress, and appearance to approved food and merchandise suppliers to participation in advertising, sales promotions, and required computer systems.\27\
\27\Andrew Elmore, The Future of Fast Food Governance, Univ. of Pennsylvania Law Rev. Online (May 24, 2017), https://papers.ssrn.com/ sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2903691.
Franchisees are under immense pressure to conform with franchisor standards and directives and risk losing their businesses if they do not. This level of control and supervision meaningfully constrains and directs how franchisees conduct their day-to-day business and worker supervision. Adding to franchisees' constrictions, the American Franchise Act explicitly shields franchisors from any sort of liability for these sorts of practices when determining joint employment liability.
A Narrow Joint Employment Standard Will Harm Workers and Small
Businesses and Benefit Low-Road Employers
The American Franchise Act seeks to radically rewrite longstanding law by amending the FLSA and NLRA to dramatically narrow the standard for finding joint employer liability for franchisors and franchisees. The bill would limit the finding of joint employment liability to a franchisor's possession and exercise of ``substantial direct and immediate control'' over their franchisees' workers' terms and conditions of employment, such as their pay, hiring, firing, and scheduling. While this extremely narrow standard is problematic enough, the bill goes a step further by also creating explicit safe harbors in which certain actions that could normally be considered ``direct and immediate control, are carved out from being indicators of joint employment.
The bill would weaken enforcement under the FLSA, which also governs federal wage theft and child labor laws. By limiting FLSA liability only to franchisors that exercise ``substantial direct and immediate control,'' the American Franchise Act would allow franchisors to evade liability for unlawful business practices and technology requirements that could result in wage theft and child labor violations. Instead, the franchisee, who may be obligated to follow these unlawful practices if it wishes to comply with its franchise agreement, is left fully liable for any damages and other consequences caused by the franchisor.
This bill would also severely limit how unionized workers could effectively bargain over all of the terms and conditions of their employment under the NLRA, which provides private-sector workers the right to organize a union and collectively bargain with their employer.\28\ Under common law, the employer does not need to exercise substantial direct and immediate control in order to determine the essential terms and conditions of employment because a joint employer can limit the wages and benefits paid by the employees' direct employers through contractual arrangements, such as salary caps. By narrowing joint employment liability to only franchisors that exercise ``substantial direct and immediate control,'' workers for the franchisee would be unable to bargain with the franchisor that determines wages and other conditions, and the franchisee would be unable to meaningfully bargain with its employees on its own.
\28\See generally 29 U.S.C. Sec. 151-169.
The American Franchise Act would also create a safe harbor for franchisors to engage in worker retaliation. The bill allows franchisors to supervise a franchisee's workers--so long as it is not ``consistently and directly''\29\ exercised--and inform the franchisee of their ``opinions'' on the performance of employees, and whether they meet acceptable standards. Through this safe harbor, a franchisor could strongly encourage a franchisee to terminate a worker engaged in union organizing activity or who raises concerns about unlawful actions in the workplace and face zero consequences.
\29\The bill does not provide a definition of ``consistently and directly'' and instead only lists examples of supervision that would not constitute consistent and direct control, leaving a large degree of uncertainty regarding what qualifies as consistent and direct control. See American Franchise Act, H.R. 5267, 119th Cong. Sec. 20(a)(G)
(2025).
In sum, the American Franchise Act is bad for workers, bad for small business franchisees, and writes a blank check to big businesses to bully and control small businesses and their workers without any accountability.
Democratic Amendments Offered During the Markup of
H.R. 5267
Committee Democrats proffered two amendments to improve H.R. 5267. The first amendment would have struck the joint employment definition under the FLSA created by H.R. 5267 and replaced the joint employment definition under the NLRA with the more equitable and worker-friendly definition from the text of H.R. 20, the Protecting the Right to Organize Act.\30\ The second amendment would have established the right for franchisees to sue franchisors for damages if the franchisee is found liable for NLRA or FLSA violations due to franchisor-mandated policies or guidance. Committee Republicans rejected both amendments.

Conclusion
For the reasons stated above, all Committee Democrats present at the markup opposed H.R. 5267 when the Committee on Education and Workforce considered it on July 21, 2026. We urge the House of Representatives to do the same.
Robert C. ``Bobby'' Scott,
Ranking Member.
